title: Autoscaling endpoints for LLM inference
gist: Together AI documents how to autoscale dedicated LLM inference on inference-native metrics, arguing in-flight request count is the only leading signal that actually sees saturation; a replayed-load experiment on a Qwen3.5-9B/H100 deployment shows ttft p95 and gpu_utilization policies never scaled while client p95 sat at 3-5 seconds. Cold starts of 86-145 seconds and the absence of scale-to-zero-with-automatic-wake make min_replicas headroom, not reactive scaling, the real defense against spikes.

themes.theme: Why classic autoscaling breaks on LLM serving

insights.claim: Dedicated LLM inference billed per replica-minute forces a choice between paying for GPUs idling at 15% utilization to cover peaks and letting p95 collapse the moment traffic exceeds what replicas can batch.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Replica-minute pricing makes autoscaling policy a direct COGS line for anyone reselling inference.
insights.quote: Almost never viable, especially in the current GPU constrained environment.
insights.locator: Over- and under-provisioning are both expensive

insights.claim: LLM serving degrades nonlinearly rather than gracefully: a replica at its concurrency limit begins queueing and time-to-first-token can jump from 200ms to 15s.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Under-provisioning risk is cliff-shaped, not linear - headroom is worth more than the spreadsheet suggests.
insights.quote: a replica at its concurrency limit doesn't get "a bit slower," it starts queueing, and TTFT can blow up from 200ms to 15s.
insights.locator: Under-provision - your p95 degrades sharply

insights.claim: GPU utilization is a misleading load signal for inference because a GPU can read 60% utilized while the engine's request queue is already backing up - utilization measures arithmetic intensity, not pressure.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Fleet dashboards built on GPU utilization systematically understate saturation and hide real capacity needs.
insights.quote: A GPU can read 60% utilized while the engine's request queue is already backing up and utilization is measuring arithmetic intensity, not pressure.
insights.locator: CPU-style metrics lie about load

insights.claim: Cold starts of several minutes - node placement, downloading tens of gigabytes of weights, VRAM load and warmup - mean a traffic spike cannot be answered after it arrives, so autoscalers must fire on leading signals.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Reactive autoscaling cannot protect an inference SLO; capacity shape has to be pre-committed.
insights.quote: you can't scale your way out of a spike because by the time it arrives it’s already too late to scale up
insights.locator: Cold starts can take several minutes

themes.theme: Proportional control loop and asymmetric windows

insights.claim: Together AI's inference autoscaler is a proportional control loop - desired replicas = ceil(N x observed/target) - damped by timing windows, clamped to replica bounds and then handed to GPU placement, with the traffic split following capacity automatically.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A proportional loop means metric and target choice, not the algorithm, determine behavior - that is where tuning leverage sits.
insights.locator: How it works

insights.claim: The recommended window asymmetry for inference autoscaling is eager scale-up and patient scale-down (default scale_down_window 5m), because a false scale-up costs a few replica-minutes while a false scale-down costs a cold start plus user-facing latency.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: The cost function is asymmetric, so symmetric default autoscaling configs are systematically wrong for LLM serving.
insights.quote: Up-window mistakes cost dollars while down-window mistakes cost latency and dollars
insights.locator: This asymmetric tradeoff of an eager up and patient down

insights.claim: A sawtooth replica count is the diagnostic signature of a scale-down window shorter than the traffic's natural rhythm, and the fix is widening the down-window - trading a few replica-minutes to eliminate repeated cold starts.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Cheap operational tell: sawtooth replica graphs mean you are paying for cold starts twice over.
insights.quote: Bursty traffic + 1-minute down-window = scale down in every trough, cold start in every crest.
insights.locator: Why does my replica count look like a sawtooth?

themes.theme: Metric catalog: leading, trailing and cost-first signals

insights.claim: Together AI exposes eight autoscaling metrics split into concurrency-driven (leading), SLO-driven (trailing) and efficiency-driven (cost-first) families, and when several are attached only the first in the list is actually used.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Multi-metric policies give a false sense of coverage - only the first metric governs behavior.
insights.locator: Under the hood: metrics to autoscale on

insights.claim: In-flight request count is the recommended default autoscaling signal because it rises before latency visibly degrades and maps onto how engines batch, with a target of about eight concurrent requests per replica - raised for short-prompt chat that batches well, lowered for long-context coding-agent traffic.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Target-8 is the anchor; workload prompt length is the variable that should move it.
insights.locator: Concurrency-driven (inflight_requests) is a safe default

insights.claim: Per-token autoscaling metrics - ttft, decoding_speed and throughput_per_replica - are only emitted on the streaming path, so deployments whose clients do not stream have no data behind those policies, with e2e_latency the exception.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: A non-streaming client base silently disables most latency-based autoscaling policies.
insights.locator: per-token metrics need streaming traffic

insights.claim: Latency SLO metrics are trailing indicators - by the time p95 TTFT breaches its threshold users have already noticed - so latency-based policies should be paired with honest headroom in min_replicas, while utilization targets near 100% leave no headroom for arrival bursts at all.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Scaling on an SLO metric guarantees you breach the SLO before you scale; buy headroom instead.
insights.locator: SLO-driven metrics (ttft, e2e_latency)

themes.theme: Cold-start budget and the absence of scale-to-zero

insights.claim: The platform offers no scale-to-zero with automatic wake - requests to a stopped deployment return an error rather than triggering a start - so idle shutdown has to be paired with explicit restart windows.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Serverless-style zero-idle economics are unavailable here; budget a floor replica for anything with real callers.
insights.locator: Idle shutdown and cold starts

insights.claim: Measured cold starts on warm 1xH100 clusters: 86s from create to replica READY for a base catalog Qwen3.5-9B, 145s for a custom fine-tune with fresh 18GB weights, a further 26-40s before the first token is served through routing, about 2.5 minutes for a 1-to-2 replica scale-up and 1-2 minutes to restart from STOPPED.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Concrete minutes-scale numbers for sizing headroom and judging whether auto-stop pays off at all.
insights.locator: we present what we got across runs on 1×H100 replicas

insights.claim: Auto-stop only pays off when idle gaps are long relative to restart time and the first user after idle tolerates an explicit start or an error-then-retry, restricting it to dev and staging; anything with a p95 SLO or unattended callers should keep min_replicas at 1.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Idle-shutdown savings are structurally unavailable to production inference workloads.
insights.locator: Notice that these windows are measured in minutes

insights.claim: When traffic can spike 10x in 90 seconds against a 4-minute cold start, the only defenses are min_replicas headroom or a higher-target policy holding slack capacity - a capacity-shape decision to settle before launch rather than a tuning knob.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Spike-to-cold-start ratio is the single number that decides whether autoscaling can protect a service at all.
insights.quote: if your traffic can spike 10× in 90 seconds and your cold start is 4 minutes, the only defenses are min_replicas headroom or a higher-target policy that keeps slack capacity up
insights.locator: A spike arrives faster than a cold start

themes.theme: Replayed-load experiment: only the queue signal fired

insights.claim: In a controlled replay on a Qwen3.5-9B deployment (1xH100 per replica, bounds 1-3, a sine wave between ~12 and ~48 RPS with two 80 RPS spikes), only the inflight_requests target-8 policy scaled - 1 to 2 to 3 replicas and 26 replica-minutes - while ttft p95 at 300ms and gpu_utilization at 75% never scaled and used 18 replica-minutes each.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Same load, same hardware, three policies - metric choice alone decided whether capacity ever moved.
insights.locator: Autoscaling the same load with various policies

insights.claim: Engine-side TTFT stayed under a 300ms target while client-side p95 ran at 3-5 seconds, because continuous batching absorbs queue pressure into total latency rather than first-token latency - so a TTFT-based policy reads healthy on a saturated system.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: TTFT SLOs are blind to the failure mode that actually hurts users on batched inference.
insights.quote: continuous batching by the engine absorbs queue pressure into total latency, not first-token latency
insights.locator: Only the concurrency signal fired

insights.claim: Short, bursty requests kept the GPU below a 75% utilization bar throughout a saturating load, so the utilization policy never triggered - both the latency and utilization signals looked healthy while the system was saturated.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Utilization-based capacity planning under bursty agentic traffic will chronically under-provision.
insights.quote: Both policies were reading signals that looked healthy while the system was saturated.
insights.locator: gpu_utilization never scaled because short, bursty requests

insights.claim: The scaling run completed 40.6k requests with 536 errors while the two non-scaling runs completed 46.4k and 46.5k requests with 6 and 2 errors respectively, even though the added capacity visibly lowered p95 mid-window.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: Scaling events are not free - the run that added replicas also carried two orders of magnitude more errors.
insights.locator: Policy table: Scaled? / Replica-minutes / Requests (errors)

insights.claim: Knowing a single replica's saturation point is prerequisite to picking an autoscaling policy: one replica here served 12-48 RPS at 3-5s p95 without falling over, which is workable for batch-style use and a non-starter against a 500ms SLO.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
insights.so_what: The per-replica saturation curve is the missing input in most inference capacity models.
insights.quote: Know your replica's saturation point before selecting a policy.
insights.locator: Three lessons from the above runs

source_meta.author: Zain Hasan, SoYoung Park, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
